summary:
(Version française plus bas.)

"Find the Moon on Earth" ranks Earth sites as analogs of the lunar south pole for a chosen mission: rover mobility, instrument calibration, a self-sufficient base, or free criteria. It scores 37 sites on 18 parameters from 8 open sources (NASA POWER, MODIS, Copernicus DEM, USGS, Smithsonian GVP) against LRO LOLA and Diviner values. Each site card shows what matches, what does not and what Earth cannot reproduce. A screening tool: 9 of 11 validation checks met, every rank with a stability range, and 27 lesser-studied candidates worth field validation. Mars comes next.

"Trouver la Lune sur Terre" classe des sites terrestres comme analogues du pôle Sud lunaire selon la mission : mobilité des rovers, calibration d'instruments, base autosuffisante ou critères libres. Il note 37 sites sur 18 paramètres issus de 8 sources ouvertes, face aux données LRO LOLA et Diviner. Chaque fiche montre ce qui concorde, ce qui ne concorde pas et ce que la Terre ne reproduit pas. Un outil de présélection : 9 attentes de validation sur 11 atteintes et 27 sites peu étudiés à valider sur le terrain. Mars suivra.
details:
Before a rover ever touches the lunar south pole, it has to learn to drive somewhere. For decades, that "somewhere" has been a handful of famous places: the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, the lava fields of Iceland. They work. But they are few, often remote, and heavily studied. So we asked a simple question: what if Earth holds many more rehearsal stages that nobody has looked at yet?

RehEARTHsal is our answer. Instead of asking which place looks like the Moon, it asks which place is good enough for a specific test. An engineer preparing a rover needs matching slopes and roughness. A scientist calibrating an instrument cares about temperature and thermal behaviour. A team planning a habitat looks at temperature extremes and ground stability. The app offers these three mission scenarios, plus a custom mode where users set their own parameters, ranges and weights.

Behind the map, every result is grounded in data. We built a reference profile of the lunar south pole from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA, Diviner, LEND). For each candidate site on Earth, the app then queries open data live: NASA POWER for climate, Copernicus DEM for slope and roughness, MODIS for surface temperature and vegetation, USGS for earthquakes and the Smithsonian for volcanoes. Nothing is stored, so every score comes straight from the sources. Each site gets an overall score, a score per criterion, and an honest card showing what matches and what doesn't. No place on Earth reproduces reduced gravity, vacuum or lunar radiation, and we say so.

To keep ourselves honest, we checked the engine like scientists. Well-known analogues should rise to the top, and the Amazon rainforest, our negative control, should sink to the bottom. Only then are the overlooked sites the tool surfaces worth a closer look, and potentially cheaper, closer places to rehearse.

RehEARTHsal is also the story of a team. We are six people in Montréal, and most of us had never met before this hackathon. What brought us together was the challenge itself: the idea that our own planet could help prepare the next steps into space. Over one weekend, strangers became a crew, each bringing a different piece: infrastructure, data, interface, robotics and instruments expertise, user experience, and security. React, TypeScript and Leaflet power the interface; Node.js and Express sit behind an OpenAPI contract; Docker and Terraform deploy it on Azure. Security is built in: no secrets in the repository, restricted CORS and rate limiting. Claude and Microsoft Copilot helped us research, write and code, and AI-generated images are watermarked.

The Moon is our first stage. The same engine is designed to welcome Mars next, and one day other worlds. After all, every journey into space begins with a rehearsal here on Earth, and sometimes with a team that has just met.
